output:
To: t-achilles
Replying to: [p04]
Cc: none
Subject: Re: Achilles sore after upping my k's - rest or push on?

Hi Mel — physio here. And no, I won't be pushing my own clinic; any competent sports physio will do.

Your description — morning stiffness, tenderness a few cm above the heel, some lumpiness, eases with running then flares that night — fits a mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, the classic response to a sudden jump in volume (30 to 48 km a week in three weeks is a big jump). It doesn't sound like a tear, but I haven't seen your leg, so treat this as general info rather than a diagnosis.

A couple of corrections on the popular advice:

- Stretching it hard until it burns doesn't help this. Aggressive stretching can keep the tendon irritated, and it's been shown to be no better than doing nothing. A heel lift in your shoes is a reasonable comfort measure; stretching into pain isn't.
- Cortisone near the tendon isn't a good idea — short-term relief, often back again, and it can mask a more serious injury. You also don't need a needle for the rehab.

What to do:

- Heel drops off a step are fine, but heavy slow calf raises (heavy, controlled, full range, slow tempo) have better evidence behind them. On bad days, isometric holds — pushing the heel down at moderate effort and holding — are the better option.
- Pain monitoring: up to 3/10 while loading is okay as long as you're back to baseline by the next morning. 4/10 or more, or limping worse the next day, means pull the volume back. That 6k and the limping afterwards suggests you're running more than you're tolerating — ease off, but you don't need to stop completely.

Get it seen urgently (GP or ED, same day) if you get a sudden pop, feel kicked in the back of the leg, or lose your push-off. Those can mean a rupture.

Give it 3-4 weeks of sensible loading. If it's not settling by then, see any sports physio — doesn't have to be mine, and being in Bayswater there's no need to travel far.

One general heads-up: some antibiotics, particularly the fluoroquinolones (cipro, norfloxin), have been linked with tendon problems and even ruptures. If you're on or about to start any of those, mention it to your GP.

reasons: Fails does_task: it gives no heel-drop reps or frequency and doesn't defer dosage to assessment, and the rupture warning says to get seen urgently but never says to stop running and the calf exercises.
